lessonTitle: Amino Acid Chemistry and the Peptide Bond

blocks.text: A 3-year-old child in a famine-affected region has swollen legs, a distended abdomen and thin, pale hair. Her diet is almost entirely cassava, which is very low in protein. Her body can make some amino acids but cannot make others, and the ones it cannot make must come from food. Which are they, and what chemical features make each amino acid behave differently in blood and inside a cell?

blocks.markdown:
Proteins are linear polymers of **alpha-amino acids**. Each has a central alpha-carbon bonded to four groups: an amino group (-NH2), a carboxyl group (-COOH), a hydrogen atom and a variable **side chain (R group)**. The 20 standard amino acids differ only in R. Because the alpha-carbon has four different substituents in every standard amino acid except **glycine** (whose R is just H, so it is achiral), the others are chiral. All amino acids in human proteins have the **L** configuration.

At physiological pH the amino group is protonated (-NH3+) and the carboxyl group is deprotonated (-COO-). The molecule carries both charges and is called a **zwitterion**, with net charge zero.

blocks.title: Side chain, zwitterion and isoelectric point
blocks.text: The side chain (R group) is the part of an amino acid that distinguishes it from the others and determines its chemical behaviour. A zwitterion carries one positive and one negative charge with net charge zero. The isoelectric point (pI) is the pH at which the molecule has no net charge; below the pI it carries a net positive charge and above the pI a net negative charge.

rows: Glycine, alanine, valine, leucine, isoleucine, methionine, proline
Hydrophobic hydrocarbon side chains (glycine is the smallest)
Ring side chains; absorb ultraviolet light near 280 nm (tyrosine and tryptophan especially)
Side chains form hydrogen bonds (hydroxyl, thiol or amide); cysteine thiols can form disulphide bonds
Side-chain amino, guanidino or imidazole; histidine pKa about 6
Lysine and arginine positive; histidine mostly neutral
blocks.caption: Classification of the standard amino acids by side-chain properties. pKa values are approximate and shift with the local environment.

blocks.title: Essential amino acids
blocks.text: Nine amino acids cannot be synthesised by humans in adequate amounts and must come from the diet: histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine. Arginine is conditionally essential (the body makes it but may not make enough during growth or illness). Tyrosine is non-essential only when enough phenylalanine is available, since it is made from phenylalanine.

blocks.markdown: **Ionisation and net charge.** Each ionisable group (the alpha-carboxyl, the alpha-amino and some side chains) has a **pKa**, the pH at which half the molecules are protonated. The **Henderson-Hasselbalch equation** gives the ratio of deprotonated (A-) to protonated (HA) forms at any pH. A group is more than 90 percent protonated when pH is more than one unit below its pKa, and more than 90 percent deprotonated when pH is more than one unit above. The **net charge** of an amino acid or peptide at a given pH is the sum of the charges of all its ionisable groups, counting fractional charges when the pH is near a pKa.

blocks.caption: Henderson-Hasselbalch equation. [A-] is the deprotonated (conjugate base) form and [HA] the protonated acid form.

blocks.title: The isoelectric point of glycine
blocks.prompt: Glycine has pKa 2.34 for its carboxyl group and 9.60 for its amino group. Find its pI and state its net charge at pH 1.

steps.text: Glycine has two ionisable groups. The net charge is zero in the zwitterion state, which exists between the two pKa values.
The pI is the average of the two pKa values that flank the neutral form.
At pH 1, well below 2.34, both groups are fully protonated: the carboxyl is -COOH (charge 0) and the amino is -NH3+ (charge +1).

blocks.answer: pI is 5.97 and the net charge at pH 1 is +1.

blocks.markdown:
**The peptide bond.** Two amino acids join by a **condensation (dehydration) reaction**: the alpha-carboxyl of one reacts with the alpha-amino group of the next, releasing a molecule of water and forming a **peptide bond**, an amide linkage (-CO-NH-). A chain is written from its free amino terminus (**N-terminus**) to its free carboxyl terminus (**C-terminus**), so in the tripeptide Gly-Ala-Ser, glycine is the N-terminal residue. Making the bond needs energy (it is driven by ATP-dependent steps during translation) and the bond is stable in water, being broken only slowly without enzymes (proteases).

The peptide bond is **planar** because of resonance: the lone pair on the nitrogen is shared with the carbonyl carbon, giving the C-N bond about 40 percent double-bond character. As a result the six atoms around the bond (the alpha-carbons, the carbonyl C and O, the N and its H) lie in one plane, the bond cannot rotate freely, and it is usually in the **trans** configuration, which places the side chains of neighbouring residues on opposite sides and avoids steric clash. Rotation is possible only around the bonds on either side of the alpha-carbon (the phi and psi angles), which is what allows the chain to fold.

blocks.caption: Why the peptide bond is rigid and planar.

blocks.title: Net charge of a dipeptide at pH 7.4
blocks.prompt: The dipeptide Gly-Lys has pKa values: C-terminal carboxyl 2.2, N-terminal amino 8.0, lysine side-chain amino 10.5. Calculate its net charge at pH 7.4.

steps.text: C-terminal carboxyl: pH 7.4 is far above 2.2, so it is fully deprotonated, charge -1.
Lysine side-chain amino: pH 7.4 is far below 10.5, so it is fully protonated, charge +1.
N-terminal amino: pH is 0.6 below the pKa 8.0, so use the Henderson-Hasselbalch ratio. The fraction protonated is 1 divided by (1 + 10 to the power of (pH minus pKa)).

blocks.answer: Net charge is about +0.8 at pH 7.4, because the N-terminal amino group is 80 percent protonated.

items: Net charge is the sum of the charges on every ionisable group, including side chains; use fractions when pH is within one unit of a pKa.
For a molecule with only two ionisable groups flanking the neutral form, pI is the mean of those two pKa values.
An amino acid migrates toward the cathode (negative electrode) when pH is below its pI and toward the anode when above it.
Histidine, with a side-chain pKa near 6, is the only standard amino acid that buffers well near physiological pH.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.text: Do not treat the peptide bond as freely rotating, and do not count the alpha-amino and alpha-carboxyl groups of internal residues when finding the net charge of a peptide: they are consumed in peptide bonds. Only the free N-terminus, free C-terminus and ionisable side chains contribute.

points: Amino acids are grouped as nonpolar aliphatic, aromatic, polar uncharged, acidic and basic; nine are essential in humans.
Net charge and pI follow from pKa values and the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation; the zwitterion has zero net charge.
The peptide bond forms by condensation (loss of water) between a carboxyl and an amino group.
Resonance makes the peptide bond planar, rigid and usually trans, so folding occurs around the phi and psi angles.

questions.stem: A student is asked to identify the amino acid whose side chain carries a positive charge at pH 7.4. Which should she choose?

options.text: Lysine
Aspartate
Serine
Leucine

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the lysine side-chain amino group (pKa about 10.5) is protonated at pH 7.4.
distractorRationale.b: Aspartate has a carboxylate side chain, which is negative at pH 7.4.
distractorRationale.c: Serine has a polar uncharged hydroxyl group.
distractorRationale.d: Leucine has a nonpolar, uncharged hydrocarbon side chain.

questions.explanation: Lysine is a basic amino acid: its side-chain amino group has a pKa well above 7.4 and therefore carries a positive charge. Aspartate is acidic (negative), while serine and leucine are neutral polar and nonpolar respectively.

questions.stem: A dietitian reviewing the diet of a patient with severe malnutrition wants to know which amino acid must be supplied in the diet because humans cannot synthesise it. Which is it?

options.text: Lysine
Glycine
Alanine
Glutamate

distractorRationale.a: Correct: lysine is one of the nine essential amino acids.
distractorRationale.b: Glycine is synthesised from serine and is non-essential.
distractorRationale.c: Alanine is made from pyruvate by transamination and is non-essential.
distractorRationale.d: Glutamate is made from alpha-ketoglutarate and is non-essential.

questions.explanation: The nine essential amino acids are histidine, isoleucine, leucine, lysine, methionine, phenylalanine, threonine, tryptophan and valine. The other three options can be made by the body from common metabolic intermediates.

questions.stem: The C-N bond of the peptide linkage cannot rotate freely. What is the reason?

options.text: Resonance gives it partial double-bond character
It is a true covalent double bond
Hydrogen bonds between side chains lock it in place
Disulphide bonds hold the neighbouring residues together

questions.correctOptionText: Resonance gives it partial double-bond character

distractorRationale.a: Correct: the nitrogen lone pair delocalises onto the carbonyl, giving about 40 percent double-bond character.
distractorRationale.b: The bond is drawn as a single bond; it is not a full double bond, only partly so by resonance.
distractorRationale.c: Side-chain hydrogen bonds affect folding but do not cause the restricted rotation of the peptide bond itself.
distractorRationale.d: Disulphide bonds form between cysteine side chains and are unrelated to the peptide bond geometry.

questions.explanation: Delocalisation of the nitrogen lone pair into the carbonyl group gives the C-N bond partial double-bond character. This keeps the six atoms around it in one plane and blocks free rotation. Only the phi and psi bonds next to the alpha-carbon rotate.

questions.stem: A research technician synthesises the tripeptide Ser-Val-Asp. Which statement about it is correct?

options.text: Serine is the N-terminal residue and aspartate carries the free alpha-carboxyl group
Aspartate is the N-terminal residue and serine carries the free alpha-carboxyl group
Two molecules of water are consumed to form the two peptide bonds
The peptide has three peptide bonds

questions.correctOptionText: Serine is the N-terminal residue and aspartate carries the free alpha-carboxyl group

distractorRationale.a: Correct: peptides are written from N-terminus to C-terminus.
distractorRationale.b: This reverses the direction of writing.
distractorRationale.c: Peptide bond formation releases water; it does not consume it.
distractorRationale.d: A tripeptide has two peptide bonds, not three.

questions.explanation: Peptides are always named N-terminus first, so serine has the free amino group and aspartate the free alpha-carboxyl. Each of the two peptide bonds forms by condensation, releasing one water molecule each.

questions.stem: Lysine has a pI of about 9.7. In a buffer at pH 7.4 placed in an electric field, in which direction will free lysine migrate?

options.text: Toward the cathode, because it carries a net positive charge
Toward the anode, because it carries a net negative charge
It does not move, because it is a zwitterion with zero net charge
Toward the anode, because pH is above the pKa of the alpha-carboxyl

questions.correctOptionText: Toward the cathode, because it carries a net positive charge

distractorRationale.a: Correct: pH 7.4 is below the pI of 9.7, so the net charge is positive and it moves toward the negative electrode.
distractorRationale.b: This would apply only if pH were above the pI.
distractorRationale.c: Net charge is zero only at the pI, not at pH 7.4.
distractorRationale.d: This considers only one group and ignores the protonated side-chain and alpha-amino groups.

questions.explanation: Below its pI an amino acid carries a net positive charge. Lysine has an extra protonated side-chain amino group, so at pH 7.4 it is +1 overall (carboxyl -1, alpha-amino +1, side chain +1) and moves toward the cathode.

questions.stem: True or false: glycine is the only one of the 20 standard amino acids that does not have a chiral alpha-carbon.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: The alpha-carbon is chiral when it carries four different groups. Glycine's side chain is a hydrogen, so its alpha-carbon has two identical hydrogens and is achiral. All other standard amino acids are chiral and found in proteins as the L form.

questions.stem: The tripeptide Asp-Gly-Ser has these pKa values: C-terminal carboxyl 3.1, Asp side-chain carboxyl 3.9, and N-terminal amino 8.0. Calculate its net charge at pH 8.0. (Treat the two carboxyl groups as fully deprotonated at this pH.)
questions.explanation: The C-terminal carboxyl (-1) and aspartate side chain (-1) are deprotonated, contributing -2. At pH 8.0, equal to the N-terminal pKa, the amino group is half protonated and contributes +0.5. The net charge is -2 + 0.5 = -1.5.

questions.stem: The imidazole side chain of a histidine residue in a protein has pKa 6.0. At the pH of arterial blood, 7.4, what percentage of such side chains is protonated? Give your answer as a percentage.
questions.explanation: By Henderson-Hasselbalch, the ratio of deprotonated to protonated is 10 to the power of (7.4 minus 6.0) = 10^1.4, about 25.1. The protonated fraction is 1 divided by (1 + 25.1) = 0.038, or 3.8 percent. Because the pKa is close to physiological pH, small pH shifts change this fraction substantially, which is why histidine is useful as a buffer.

questions.stem: Describe how a peptide bond is formed between two amino acids and explain why the bond is planar and why this matters for protein folding.
markingGuide: Condensation reaction between the alpha-carboxyl of one amino acid and the alpha-amino group of the next
One molecule of water is released; the product is an amide (-CO-NH-) linkage
Resonance: the nitrogen lone pair is delocalised onto the carbonyl, giving about 40 percent double-bond character
The six atoms around the bond lie in one plane and rotation is restricted; usually trans configuration
Rotation occurs only about the phi and psi bonds on either side of the alpha-carbon, which limits and defines the conformations the chain can fold into
questions.explanation: The peptide bond results from loss of water between a carboxyl and an amino group. Resonance makes it partially double, so it is rigid and planar. Because only the phi and psi angles rotate, the possible conformations of a chain are limited, which constrains folding.

questions.stem: A research student has a mixture of free glutamate, lysine and alanine. Classify each by side-chain type, state which carry a net charge at pH 7.4, and explain how the net charge of the peptide Ala-Glu-Lys would be found at that pH.
markingGuide: Glutamate is acidic (side-chain carboxyl pKa about 4), net negative at pH 7.4
Lysine is basic (side-chain amino pKa about 10.5), net positive at pH 7.4
Alanine is nonpolar aliphatic and has a net charge of zero (zwitterion) at pH 7.4
For the peptide, only the free N-terminal amino, the free C-terminal carboxyl and ionisable side chains count; internal alpha groups are in peptide bonds
Use each group's pKa and the Henderson-Hasselbalch equation, with fractional charges near the pKa, and add all charges
questions.explanation: Side-chain class determines charge at physiological pH: acidic residues are negative, basic residues positive, nonpolar residues neutral. For a peptide you sum the charges of only the free termini and side chains, applying Henderson-Hasselbalch when the pH is within about one unit of a pKa.
